title: Thou art the man (2 Samuel 12:1–7)
hookLine: Nathan's parable of the poor man's ewe lamb ends "Thou art the man"
carry: the judge has written his own verdict

cards: A prophet walks into the palace with a case for the king to judge. That's all it looks like. Nathan doesn't mention a rooftop, or a soldier, or a letter carried to the front.
He tells a story about two men in one city. One is rich, with flocks and herds. The other has nothing at all except one little ewe lamb.
The king leans in to listen, the way a judge listens. He has no idea the story is about him. By the time he finds out, he has already passed sentence.

teach.h: THE LAMB WAS LIKE A DAUGHTER.
teach.b: Hear how Nathan builds the lamb. The poor man bought her and raised her with his children. She ate from his own bread, drank from his own cup, slept in his arms.

She was to him like a daughter. Every detail makes her harder to lose. Then a traveler comes to the rich man, who won't take from his own flock, so he takes the poor man's lamb and serves her for dinner.

David's anger burns. As the Lord lives, he says, the man who did this deserves to die, and he shall pay back the lamb fourfold, because he had no pity. And Nathan answers, short and plain: "Thou art the man."
Why a story? A king who can arrange a death at the front is not an easy man to accuse. So Nathan goes around the defenses.
He lets David's sense of justice wake up about someone else, where it's easy, and then turns it around. The judge has written his own verdict.
The parable can't carry all of it: in what David actually did there was a woman, and a husband who was killed, and Nathan doesn't pretend otherwise.
Right after the story he speaks plainly, in God's name: you had everything, and if that were too little, more would have been given. Why did you despise the word of the Lord?
Plain speech walks through it. David is still the king, with every power to silence the man in front of him. Everything now turns on whether he will listen.

how: Jews read Nathan's parable as part of the book of Samuel, among the Former Prophets, and some teachers use it as a model of how to rebuke someone with care, so that they can actually hear it.

o: a riddle with a hidden word for its answer
a law the king must keep when he judges
a story that lets a listener judge himself

games.q: thou art the man — tap the pairs.
p: passes sentence on the rich man

s: Nathan accused David directly from the start
he began with a case about two men in one city, and let David judge it first.
David sentenced the rich man before he knew who he was
he said the man deserved to die and must repay the lamb fourfold.
right after it, he spoke plainly in God's name about what David had done.

games.q: you're Nathan. you've been sent to tell a king, who can arrange a death at the front, that he has done evil. how do you begin?
o: accuse him to his face, at once.
tell him a story and let him judge it.
say nothing and hope someone else does.
games.why: Nathan tells the story of the ewe lamb. David's own anger passes the sentence, and then Nathan says: thou art the man.

practice: Bring to mind one person who sees you clearly, someone who doesn't flatter, and something they might say that you'd rather not hear.
Let it sit in the room without arguing back, and notice where in your body the defenses rise; breathe into that spot. If you pray, you can ask for ears that can hear.

wordCard.voice: Parable. The story Nathan told the king, about a rich man and a poor man's ewe lamb, to make him judge himself. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: you are the man, Nathan's words to David in 2 Samuel 12:7.

carryVoice: Your line: the judge has written his own verdict. Sometimes the story is about us. That's day seven hundred forty-seven.
